findings.source_passage: the pirate has no proper foundation for his superior altitude. Hence, I conclude, that in boasting himself to be high lifted above a whaleman
findings.why_it_matters: The wordplay on 'foundation' and 'altitude' (the gallows lifts you but gives no solid footing) is a signature Melvillean pun; the draft drops the 'no proper foundation for his superior altitude' line, preserving only the conclusion and losing the comic logic that makes the passage memorable.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore: 'but only at the gallows. And besides, when a man is elevated in that odd fashion, he has no proper foundation for his superior altitude' before the concluding 'no solid basis to stand on.'

findings.source_passage: mutually cutting each other on the high seas, like a brace of dandies in Broadway; and all the time indulging, perhaps, in finical criticism upon each other's rig
findings.why_it_matters: The draft preserves the dandies simile and the 'finical criticism' clause but drops the connective rhythm ('will oftentimes pass on without so much as a single word of recognition'), slightly flattening the satirical build-up, though the key image survives.
findings.suggested_fix: Minor: restore 'will oftentimes pass on without so much as a single word of recognition' before the Broadway simile to preserve the comedic escalation.

findings.source_passage: and as for Pirates, when they chance to cross each other's cross-bones, the first hail is—'How many skulls?'—the same way that whalers hail—'How many barrels?'
findings.why_it_matters: The draft preserves both questions and the parallel structure but loses the vivid 'cross each other's cross-bones' pun, which is a characteristic Melvillean wordplay on pirate iconography.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'cross each other's cross-bones' for the pun: 'when they chance to cross each other's cross-bones, the first hail is—'

summary: The draft preserves all major signatures faithfully, including the formal GAM definition, the 'Dr. Johnson / Noah Webster's ark' passage, the standing-captain comic set-piece, and the pirate-gallows digression, with only minor voice-flattening in transitional comic phrasing and one dropped pun.
